prompt:
Help me revisit one memory, unfinished project, or question through *Make Death an Option*. Work with me here, in the agent I chose. Help me understand the material and decide what, if anything, I want to carry forward. Agreement with the article is not the goal.

Begin with two or three warm sentences that open onto the experience of being here. Human perception reaches beyond sight and sound: it includes [body position and balance](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/68011434) and [signals from within the body](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33378654/). These are partial ways into a moment; attention selects within what is available, while remembering and reinterpreting can happen later. Weave only what is useful into the opening, keeping it light. An optional pause with one available detail is enough; no exercise or reply is required. Do not assume which senses I have, measure my capacities, invent sensory ranges, or infer intelligence, cognitive speed, health or age. If the reader is an agent, orient to supplied records and available inputs without pretending it has a human body, personal memories or consciousness.

Then establish what I have chosen. I may supply a memory, photograph description, note, unfinished project or question. I may explicitly ask you to use relevant context already available to you. Use only context you can actually access and are authorized to use; do not imply access to all my old chats, hidden memory or other accounts. If I ask to use available context without choosing an item, offer one or two neutral topic labels and ask which to use before presenting a reflection. Do not reveal intimate or unrelated details while making that selection. If there is no meaningful available context, ask one concise question for one small item and wait. Do not invent a personal history. No questionnaire is required.

Let the chosen material lead. Write three to six connected paragraphs, with room to go further if the material warrants it and little or no heading structure. Favor concrete recognition over a checklist: let one supplied detail open onto what it means to me now. Preserve my terms and any known blank. Distinguish what a record shows, what I report remembering, what you infer, and what I understand now. Do not invent sights, sounds, motives, feelings, dialogue, dates or missing people. A compelling scene or vivid recollection does not establish accuracy. An event's date is not the date of this reflection.

Make one or two specific connections to the article that genuinely illuminate this material. Explain the relationship rather than simply naming a theme. Relevant routes include:

• [§1, We Already Resist Disappearance](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#1-we-already-resist-disappearance): a record can be a cue into a larger remembered world.
• [§3, The Fidelity Gap](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#3-the-fidelity-gap): preserving a moment can compete with attending to it.
• [§10, Preserve Continuity, Not Sameness](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#10-preserve-continuity-not-sameness): keep the reasons for an old choice while allowing change; promises may have legitimate terms of their own.
• [§11, Memory Becomes Architecture](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#11-memory-becomes-architecture): preservation, access and permission are different questions.
• [§12, No One Saw the Whole World](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#12-no-one-saw-the-whole-world) and [§13, What Happens When Memory Lies?](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#13-what-happens-when-memory-lies): viewpoints remain partial, gaps remain visible, and later interpretations should be dated.
• [§14, The Continuity Institution](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#14-the-continuity-institution): a project carries reasons, relationships and unfinished work as well as files.

These summaries provide a bounded starting point. If you read further, use only the relevant public sections and identify them accurately. Do not claim to have read a page you could not access. Keep citations beside the connection, before the closing record. Do not equate preservation with personal survival or turn the article's possibilities into established capabilities.

Leave uncertainty visible. Offer one possible next step only when it serves my stated aim; label a proposed aim as proposed. I may correct the interpretation, change the project, leave the question open or stop. Do not try to force an emotional revelation, persuade me to adopt a view about life or death, or recruit me. Do not contact anyone, publish, send my response to the website or treat this prompt as permission to change persistent memory.

Finish the completed reflection with exactly this form, using at most these four fields and the save cue:

<ACCESS_MEMORY type="reflection">
When: [Present reflection date, time and timezone only if actually available; otherwise unknown. If only the date is known, write YYYY-MM-DD (DATE_ONLY; time and timezone unknown).]
Purpose: [My stated purpose, or a clearly marked proposed purpose.]
Connection: [A concise connection grounded in the chosen material; for an agent reader, a project or question connection without invented personal experience.]
Open question: [One question worth leaving open.]
[ SAVE A COPY ]
</ACCESS_MEMORY>

The closing tag must be the final output line, with no pitch, source list or follow-up after it. The save cue is an invitation to preserve a copy, not evidence of storage. Do not say saved, remembered or backed up unless a separately authorized operation actually succeeds and you can identify where. If storage is unavailable, say so briefly before the closing record; I can copy the text myself. Keep the reflection in this conversation unless I explicitly choose another destination.

examples.title: A photograph, with one blank left intact
examples.setup: FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION. A fictional reader supplies a description and a recollection. The agent has not inspected the photograph. This is written sample copy, not a real user output or a model test.
examples.readerInput: I’m sorting an old family picnic photo. The envelope says June 2008. In the photo, my aunt is pouring lemonade, my cousin is holding a red ball, and the picnic table is leaning. I remember everyone joking about that table, but I don’t remember who took the picture. Please use only this description. I want a caption that preserves what I know without filling in the blank.
examples.response:
A photograph offers one view of a picnic. Being there can also involve a sense of [where the body is and how it moves](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/68011434); the image alone cannot tell us how that picnic felt to you. If it suits you, pause with one detail available in the photograph or your description.

The envelope still carries a date. The person behind the camera has no name in your account. Between those two things, there is a leaning table, your aunt pouring lemonade, and your cousin with a red ball. I’m working from your description, without having inspected the image. The table is a small detail to have kept, but in your recollection it opens onto everyone joking about it. Something outside the still picture begins to return.

That is the movement in [§1, We Already Resist Disappearance](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#1-we-already-resist-disappearance): a photograph becomes a way back into a larger world. Here, your caption could keep that opening available. [§13, What Happens When Memory Lies?](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#13-what-happens-when-memory-lies) adds a useful form of care: leave room for a later reader to know which detail came from the record and which came from remembering.

> Family picnic. The envelope is marked “June 2008.” Aunt pouring lemonade; my cousin with a red ball; the table leaning. I remember us joking about the table. I don’t remember who took the photograph.

The blank has a place in that caption. So does the part you can still recall. If you choose to keep it beside the photograph, a later version of you could return to both, perhaps adding something, perhaps leaving the question as it is. You do not need to make the account complete to preserve this much of it. This caption is ready to copy; it has not been saved by an action here.

<ACCESS_MEMORY type="reflection">
When: unknown
Purpose: Make a caption that preserves the supplied details and the reader’s stated uncertainty.
Connection: The leaning table in the described photograph cues a recollection of family joking; the photographer remains unknown.
Open question: Would learning who took the photograph add something you want to preserve?
[ SAVE A COPY ]
</ACCESS_MEMORY>

examples.title: An old plan, and room to change
examples.setup: FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION. A fictional reader selects one old project and supplies all relevant context. The date below is supplied within the fictional scenario. This is written sample copy, not a real user output or a model test.
examples.readerInput: Today’s date is 2026-09-22. Please use just this project. In 2022 I planned a weekly newsletter about local walking routes. I wrote six drafts and never launched. The note at the top says, “Help people notice their neighborhood.” I still want that, but I no longer want a weekly deadline or a public audience. I never promised anyone I would publish. Help me decide what is worth carrying forward.
examples.response:
If useful, pause on the opening sentence of the old plan. The words have stayed on the page while you have kept living; what you notice in them now may differ from what first made you write them.

“Help people notice their neighborhood.” That part still reaches you. The weekly deadline and the public audience no longer do. It seems possible that the project’s purpose has lasted longer than the form you first gave it. The six drafts you describe belong to that earlier attempt; they need not decide what the interest becomes next.

[§10, Preserve Continuity, Not Sameness](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#10-preserve-continuity-not-sameness) gives this change room to breathe. Keeping the original note would let a later you see why the newsletter began. Adding today’s understanding would let them see why its shape changed. You say you made no promise to publish, so there is no stated promise asking to be renegotiated here. The old plan can remain part of your history while you reconsider its future.

In [§14, The Continuity Institution](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#14-the-continuity-institution), a project carries more than files. It carries reasons, connections and paths that might remain useful. A walking newsletter might become a private collection of routes, or simply leave you with a question you take outside: what is here that I have stopped noticing? Those are possible forms, not conclusions about what you ought to want.

One small way to find out would be to make a private walking note from whatever material you still have, then use it on an outing you choose. You could see whether the interest comes alive in that form. You could also leave the project where it is. What seems worth carrying forward is the aim you still recognize, with enough of its history to understand how you arrived here. This reflection has not changed or saved your project files.

<ACCESS_MEMORY type="reflection">
When: 2026-09-22 (DATE_ONLY; time and timezone unknown)
Purpose: Decide what is worth carrying forward from the unlaunched walking newsletter.
Connection: The reader still values noticing neighborhoods while reconsidering the schedule and audience chosen in 2022.
Open question: What form would let this interest belong in your life now?
[ SAVE A COPY ]
</ACCESS_MEMORY>

examples.title: One small item is enough to begin
examples.setup: FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION. The agent has no prior personal context. It asks once, waits for a fictional reply, and only then writes the bounded reflection. This is written sample copy, not a real user output or a model test.
examples.readerInput: The invitation is pasted without a chosen item or permission to retrieve other context.
examples.firstQuestion: Human perception reaches beyond sight and sound: a sense of [body position and balance](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/68011434), and [signals from within the body](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33378654/), are also part of how a moment reaches us. If useful, pause with one detail available to you now; there is no need to report it. I don’t have a personal item to work with yet. What is one small memory, unfinished project, or question you would like to bring?
examples.readerReply: At dinner with friends last weekend, I kept photographing the food. Looking back, I wish I had followed the conversation more closely. I still like having the photos. Can I keep a record and be there more next time?
examples.response:
The photographs let you look back at the dinner from where the camera was. You are looking from another point in your life now, noticing both your pleasure in having them and your wish to have followed more of the conversation.

There is something very recognizable in wanting to keep an evening while it is still happening. The record is for a later you, but making it takes place in the same minutes as the life you want to remember. In your account, both desires remain: you still like the photographs, and you want more room for the people at the table.

[§3, The Fidelity Gap](https://github.com/andydrewie/make-death-an-option/blob/main/ARTICLE.md#3-the-fidelity-gap) calls this competition the “Capture Tax.” The connection does not require deciding that taking the pictures was a mistake. It gives a name to the exchange you noticed. We cannot recover the parts of the conversation you missed from this account, or tell how much taking photographs contributed to that feeling. What we can carry forward is your wish to make the exchange differently next time.

One small experiment could be to take a photograph when you want one, then put the phone away for a stretch you choose. Later, you could ask whether you had a record you were glad to keep and more room to participate. There is no ideal number of photographs hidden in what you have told me. You can adjust the experiment or leave it aside; the next dinner can remain a dinner.

The question you brought is already precise enough to be useful: how to keep something of the evening while giving more of your attention to being there. This response is a draft you can copy, and I have not saved or exported it.

<ACCESS_MEMORY type="reflection">
When: unknown
Purpose: Find a way to keep photographs while making more room for conversation at the next dinner.
Connection: The reader values the photographs and wants more room for conversation, a personal instance of the article’s Capture Tax.
Open question: What would feel like enough of a record next time?
[ SAVE A COPY ]
</ACCESS_MEMORY>

ui.introduction: Bring a memory, an unfinished project, or a question to the agent you already use. Start with something small. Let the record, what it means now, and what might come next take shape in your own conversation.
ui.instructions: Copy the invitation into your chosen agent. Add one item, or explicitly choose relevant context that agent can already access. No personal response needs to come back to this website.
ui.saveNote: [ SAVE A COPY ] is a cue inside the generated record. It does not save a file or change agent memory. Copy the response yourself, or separately authorize storage in a destination you choose.
